articles.title: Keeping a household meter-reading record
articles.summary: Create a private record of water, gas and electricity meter readings without handling live equipment.

sections.title: Identify the meter safely
paragraphs: Use the supplier account or tenancy documents to establish which meter belongs to the household; flats may have meters in shared or locked cupboards. Do not open electrical cabinets, remove seals or enter restricted service spaces to find a meter.

A meter identifier and its displayed reading are different things. Check the supplier's instructions for the correct units and register layout, particularly where the display cycles through several screens.

sections.title: Record consistently
paragraphs: When a meter can be viewed safely and access is authorised, note the date, displayed digits, units and whether the reading was estimated or observed. A private photograph may help resolve later transcription mistakes.
Keep personal account numbers and property identifiers in a protected household record, not in a public guide or shared community post.

sections.title: Investigate discrepancies
paragraphs: Compare successive readings with supplier statements over a meaningful period; seasonal use and tariff changes can affect bills even when equipment is working normally.
If the reading seems implausible or the display is damaged, contact the supplier or responsible building manager rather than attempting to reset, dismantle or repair the meter.

articles.title: Building an offline appliance manual index
articles.summary: Make product instructions, model identifiers and service contacts easy to retrieve during an outage.

visual.alt: A three-row checklist showing how an appliance model is linked to its locally stored manual and periodically reviewed.
visual.caption: Illustrative document organisation, not appliance operating instructions.

sections.title: Locate the right documents
paragraphs: List household equipment that has safety, cleaning, filter or maintenance instructions, including heating controls, ventilation, kitchen appliances and portable power products.
Record the manufacturer and exact model shown on an accessible label or purchase record. Similar-looking appliances may require different procedures, replacement parts or maintenance intervals.

sections.title: Keep offline references
paragraphs: Save permitted copies of the manufacturer's manual to a secure offline folder or retain paper copies. A simple index should describe where each document lives rather than duplicating an entire manual into an unprotected note.
Check that the saved version matches the model and language, and that the pages needed for warnings, faults and servicing are legible without a network connection.

sections.title: Review and retire
paragraphs: Update the index when equipment is replaced, serviced or moved. Note the date of a professional inspection separately from an ordinary household check.
Dispose of obsolete instructions carefully if they include account information, and keep relevant warranty or tenancy records in an appropriate private location.

articles.title: Recording condensation and damp patterns
articles.summary: Distinguish recurring moisture observations from assumptions about the underlying cause.

visual.alt: Three connected stages represent observing a damp pattern, keeping dated records and reporting persistent concerns.
visual.caption: A documentation workflow; it does not diagnose moisture or mould.

sections.title: Observe without disturbing damage
paragraphs: Note where water droplets, staining or musty odours occur and whether they follow cooking, bathing, rainfall or cold weather. A pattern can help a landlord or specialist investigate.
Avoid scraping, sanding or opening suspected damaged or mouldy materials to diagnose the problem. Water ingress, poor ventilation, leaks and building defects may have similar visible symptoms.

sections.title: Document the pattern
paragraphs: Keep dated notes and photographs of affected areas, including whether a window, extractor or radiator was in normal use. Do not record sensitive household details in a public issue report.
If safe and available, note humidity or temperature observations as context, but do not use a single consumer reading to conclude that the building is safe or that a particular defect is proven.

sections.title: Escalate persistent problems
paragraphs: Report recurring damp, significant mould, unexplained leaks or damaged surfaces to the landlord, building manager or suitable professional. Seek appropriate health advice where symptoms or vulnerability make exposure a concern.
Do not cover serious staining with paint or seal materials as a substitute for investigating the source. Follow any property-specific ventilation and maintenance instructions.

articles.title: Checking uneven room heating
articles.summary: Collect useful observations about heating performance before requesting qualified maintenance.

sections.title: Map the symptoms
paragraphs: Identify which rooms feel unusually cold or warm, whether the problem is persistent and what the thermostat or programmed schedule appears to request.
Check ordinary user controls only as described by the appliance manual. Avoid opening a boiler, altering gas components, removing covers or using unknown service settings.

sections.title: Record context
paragraphs: Note dates, occupied rooms, normal control settings and whether other hot-water or heating functions appear affected. Distinguish a heating complaint from an actual gas, smoke or carbon-monoxide warning.
A radiator that feels cool at one moment is not necessarily faulty: demand, schedules and system design vary. Avoid universal diagnoses based on a single touch or temperature reading.

sections.title: Arrange follow-up
paragraphs: Consult the appliance instructions, landlord or competent heating engineer for persistent problems. Keep emergency contact routes separate from routine service requests.
If an alarm activates, gas is suspected or combustion safety is in doubt, follow the relevant official emergency instructions rather than troubleshooting from this draft.

articles.title: Inspecting everyday door hardware
articles.summary: Spot loose, damaged or unreliable handles and latches without compromising fire safety.

visual.alt: A three-row checklist reminds the reader to identify the type of door, observe visible hardware and report concerns.
visual.caption: Do not alter fire-door or escape-door components without approval.

sections.title: Identify the door type
paragraphs: Distinguish an ordinary internal door from a fire-resisting door, communal entrance or designated escape door. Those special doors can have specific legal, building and manufacturer requirements.
Observe whether a handle returns normally, a latch engages, or visible fittings appear loose or damaged. Avoid repeatedly forcing a stuck lock or testing a suspect exit in a way that traps occupants.

sections.title: Keep an observation record
paragraphs: Note the door location, symptom, date and whether it affects access, security or an escape route. A photograph of a visible defect can help a maintenance professional understand the concern.
Do not remove self-closing devices, alter fire-door seals, wedge a fire door open or substitute generic hardware without appropriate approval.

sections.title: Prioritise repairs
paragraphs: Treat unreliable exits, fire-door defects and failed security doors as matters for prompt responsible management. Routine cosmetic wear can be tracked separately.
For rented and shared buildings, contact the responsible landlord or managing agent before changing fittings that may belong to the building.

articles.title: Recognising slow household drainage
articles.summary: Observe drainage changes and know when a problem needs plumbing or building-management help.

sections.title: Identify the affected fixtures
paragraphs: Record whether a sink, bath, shower or other fixture drains more slowly than usual, and whether multiple fixtures show problems together.
Several affected fixtures, repeated backing-up or wastewater appearing where it should not can indicate a wider issue. Avoid assuming the cause is confined to the nearest visible trap.

sections.title: Avoid risky shortcuts
paragraphs: Do not combine drain-cleaning chemicals or pour unfamiliar substances into plumbing. Chemical products may create hazardous exposure and can complicate later professional work.
Avoid dismantling concealed or communal drainage, using high-pressure tools or attempting repairs that could cause flooding or contaminate the home.

sections.title: Report and track
paragraphs: Note dates, affected rooms, odours, unusual sounds and any visible overflow. Keep children and pets away from contaminated water and arrange appropriate assistance.
If wastewater is backing up or electrical fittings are threatened, avoid contact with affected areas and seek the responsible emergency or qualified service.

articles.title: Organising compatible household spare parts
articles.summary: Keep useful consumables identifiable without buying unsafe or mismatched replacements.

visual.alt: Three labelled shelves represent matching spare parts to models, preserving packaging and checking stock.
visual.caption: Storage schematic only; it does not certify part compatibility.

sections.title: Identify before buying
paragraphs: Start with frequently replaced nonhazardous consumables, such as manufacturer-specified vacuum bags or simple removable accessories. Record the appliance's exact model and the part number from its documentation.
Do not assume that visually similar filters, fuses, seals or electrical components are interchangeable. Safety-critical replacements need manufacturer guidance and sometimes a qualified installer.

sections.title: Store with context
paragraphs: Keep unopened parts with their original packaging and labels. Note which appliance they belong to and any storage conditions specified by the manufacturer.
Avoid accumulating mystery parts without provenance. A photograph of packaging and a clear shelf location can make inventory more useful than a bare quantity count.

sections.title: Check before use
paragraphs: Inspect packaging for damage and confirm that the part still matches the equipment after repairs or replacements. Record when stock is used and remove obsolete entries.
Do not use a stored part simply because it fits physically; ratings, materials, approvals and model revisions may differ.

articles.title: Tracking landlord and contractor maintenance requests
articles.summary: Create a clear timeline of property issues, responses and completed work.

visual.alt: Three connected circles show logging a property concern, tracking correspondence and checking the outcome.
visual.caption: Keep sensitive household details in private records.

sections.title: Capture the problem
paragraphs: Record a short description, location, first observed date and practical impact. Distinguish urgent safety concerns from routine cosmetic defects without claiming a universal legal response time.
Include relevant photographs only when appropriate, and avoid placing names, access codes or personal contact information in a publicly shared issue log.

sections.title: Track responsibility and communication
paragraphs: Note when the issue was reported, to whom, any reference number and the agreed next action. Keep copies of important correspondence in a private offline folder.
A request marked sent does not prove receipt, and a contractor visit does not necessarily prove a repair is complete. Record what actually happened rather than relying only on status labels.

sections.title: Close with evidence
paragraphs: After work, note the date, the part of the problem addressed and any follow-up needed. If an issue recurs, link it to the earlier record rather than losing the history.
For safety-critical defects or disputes about responsibility, seek the relevant professional or housing advice rather than relying on a generic app checklist.
